entries.answer: I now have a comprehensive understanding of the entire technical document. It is the Seedance 2.0 technical report by ByteDance Seed (arXiv:2604.14148v1). The document is primarily an evaluation/benchmark paper describing architecture, capabilities, training philosophy, and benchmarking of a unified multimodal audiovideo generation model. My task is to rewrite the entire content as a single, comprehensive, technical construction prompt — without naming the original model — in productionready, unambiguous language.

Based on the full content of your uploaded technical report, here is the comprehensive, single, productionready construction prompt:[1]



 Construction Prompt

Build a unified, largescale, multimodal audiovideo joint generation model from scratch. The system must natively support four input modalities — text, image, audio, and video — and produce synchronized audiovideo output. Every component described below must be implemented in complete, productionready code with no placeholders, stubs, mock layers, or simplified approximations.



 1. Overall Architecture

Design a single unified transformerbased diffusion architecture that jointly generates video and audio in one forward pass. The model must not treat video and audio as separate pipelines with a posthoc fusion step. Instead, all modalities — text conditioning, image conditioning, video conditioning, audio conditioning, and the output video and audio streams — must be processed within one shared latent space and one shared set of transformer layers. The architecture must be highly efficient and scalable to large parameter counts.

The model must support the following generation tasks as firstclass capabilities, all within the same weights:

 TexttoVideo (T2V): Generate a video clip with synchronized audio from a text prompt alone.
 ImagetoVideo (I2V): Generate a video clip with synchronized audio conditioned on one or more reference images and an optional text prompt.
 ReferencetoVideo (R2V): Generate a video clip conditioned on an arbitrary combination of up to 3 video clips, up to 9 images, and up to 3 audio clips simultaneously, along with a text prompt.
 Video Editing: Accept an existing video clip and a text instruction describing a targeted modification (subject replacement, style change, scene change, audio content change) and produce a modified video where nontargeted regions are preserved with maximum consistency.
 Video Extension / Continuation: Accept an existing video clip and generate a seamless forward or backward temporal continuation aligned with a userprovided text prompt. The continuation must be temporally coherent with the input clip, without visual discontinuities at the boundary.
 Combination Tasks: Support compound tasks that pair reference and editing within a single generation pass — for example, swapping the subject of an input video with a subject drawn from a reference image while preserving the scene, motion, and audio.

All tasks above must be executable in any standalone or combinatorial configuration using one model checkpoint, not separate finetuned checkpoints per task.



 2. Output Specifications

The model must natively generate audiovideo content with the following specifications:

 Duration: 4 to 15 seconds per generation.
 Native output resolutions: 480p and 720p.
 Audio: Binaural (dualchannel) stereo output. Multitrack: background audio, ambient sound effects, and character narration/dialogue must be generated simultaneously as separate tracks that are mixed into the final output with precise temporal alignment to the visual content.
 Frame rate: Standard cinematic/broadcast frame rates (24fps minimum; support 30fps).
 Audio sample rate: CDquality minimum (44.1 kHz); professionalgrade preferred (48 kHz).



 3. Visual Tokenization and Latent Space

Implement a video variational autoencoder (VAE) that encodes raw video frames into a compressed spatiotemporal latent representation. The VAE must:

 Apply spatial and temporal downsampling to reduce the token count while preserving perceptually critical detail (fine textures, light refraction, facial microexpressions, hand geometry).
 Produce a latent space in which both 480p and 720p videos of varying durations can be represented without architectural changes — use dynamic sequence length handling, not fixedresolution heads.
 Achieve reconstruction quality sufficient that closeup shots of human faces, hands, fabric, and liquid surfaces are indistinguishable from real footage at the original resolution.
 Be jointly trained with the diffusion backbone or pretrained and frozen, depending on the training recipe described in Section 7.

Implement a corresponding audio tokenizer / codec that encodes waveforms into a compact latent sequence compatible with the video latent in terms of temporal resolution and sequence length conventions. The audio latent must carry sufficient information to reconstruct the full binaural mix.



 4. MultiModal Input Encoding

 4.1 Text Encoder

Use a large pretrained language model as the text encoder. The encoder must:

 Handle prompts of arbitrary length, including long multishot scripts with extensive character interaction descriptions, specific action sequences, camera movement directives, and stylistic aesthetic instructions.
 Preserve finegrained semantic detail throughout the encoding — compound instructions, counterfactual instructions, and abstract creative prompts must all produce distinguishable conditioning signals.
 Support multilingual input including Chinese (standard Mandarin, Sichuan dialect, Northeastern dialect, Cantonese), Chinese opera, Chinese minority languages, English, and singing/rap content. The text encoder must not degrade on nonEnglish input.

 4.2 Image Encoder

Implement a visual feature extractor (e.g., a ViTbased encoder) that encodes reference images into dense visual feature sequences. The encoder must:

 Preserve subject identity, appearance details, artistic style, special effect style, and compositional layout of the reference image.
 When up to 9 reference images are provided simultaneously, encode each independently and provide all feature sequences to the main transformer via crossattention or concatenation, without loss of perimage identity.

 4.3 Video Reference Encoder

Implement encoding of reference video clips (up to 3 clips simultaneously). The encoder must extract and preserve:

 Subject appearance and identity across frames.
 Motion rhythm and temporal dynamics.
 Cinematographic properties: shot composition, camera movement trajectory, editing rhythm.
 Special effect visual styles and plot narrative structure.

 4.4 Audio Reference Encoder

Implement encoding of reference audio clips (up to 3 clips simultaneously). The encoder must extract and preserve:

 Acoustic characteristics: timbre, prosody, singing style, instrumental texture.
 Temporal rhythm information for beat alignment with generated video.



 5. Main Diffusion Transformer

The core generative module is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates in the joint audiovideo latent space. Implement it as follows:

 5.1 Architecture

 Use a full transformer backbone (not UNet) operating on flattened spatiotemporalaudio latent token sequences.
 Implement 3D RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) or an equivalent positional encoding that encodes spatial (height, width), temporal (frame index), and audiotemporal position jointly in a unified coordinate system.
 Implement adaptive layer normalization (adaLN) conditioned on diffusion timestep and all conditioning signals.
 All crossmodal conditioning (text, image features, video reference features, audio reference features) must be injected via crossattention layers interleaved throughout the transformer depth. Do not inject conditioning only at the input or output layers.

 5.2 Unified Joint Generation

The transformer must process video latent tokens and audio latent tokens as a single concatenated sequence, with attention operating across both modalities simultaneously. Audiovisual temporal alignment must emerge from this joint attention and must not require posthoc synchronization.

 5.3 Flow Matching / Score Matching Objective

Train the transformer using a continuoustime flow matching or scorebased diffusion objective (e.g., rectified flow). Implement:

 A noise schedule appropriate for highresolution spatiotemporal generation.
 Classifierfree guidance (CFG) for all conditioning signals independently, with separate guidance scales for text, image, video reference, and audio conditioning.
 Support for negative prompting.

 5.4 MultiShot Native Generation

The architecture must inherently support multishot narrative generation without requiring external shot segmentation. The transformer must be capable of autonomously planning shot sequencing, designing transitions between shots, and maintaining subject identity across shots within a single generated clip. Implement positional encoding that enables this crossshot consistency.



 6. Audio Generation Module

Implement the audio generation module as a component integrated within the main transformer, not as a separate posthoc system. Requirements:

 Binaural spatial audio: Generate true binaural (twochannel, headrelated transfer functionaware) audio with spatial scene cues matching the visual content (e.g., sounds panning to match onscreen object positions).
 Multitrack decomposition: The generation must simultaneously produce: (1) background music/ambient audio, (2) environmental sound effects (footsteps, environmental sounds, physical interactions), and (3) character voice/dialogue/narration. These tracks must be temporally aligned with visual actions at the frame level.
 Audiovisual synchronization: Lip movements of onscreen characters must be synchronized with generated speech. Physical interactions (e.g., a hand hitting a surface) must produce sounds synchronized to the frame of contact. Beat matching between background music and visual editing rhythm must be enforced.
 Voice and acoustic reference preservation: When audio reference clips are provided, the generated audio must preserve the timbre, prosody, and vocal characteristics of the reference while adapting content to match the generated scene.



 7. Training Pipeline

 7.1 Data Pipeline

Build a largescale data preprocessing pipeline for both video and audio:

 Video data: Ingest raw video at scale. Apply scene detection and shot segmentation. Filter for visual quality: resolution, compression artifacts, motion blur, occlusion. Apply aesthetic scoring to filter for cinematic quality, composition, and lighting. Generate dense captions for each clip using a multimodal visionlanguage model. Captions must describe: subjects and their appearances, actions, interactions, camera movements, lighting, composition, and style. Generate multilingual captions.
 Audio data: Separate audio tracks using source separation. Generate audio captions describing sound events, voice characteristics, music genre, and acoustic environment. Timealign audio event labels to video frame timestamps.
 Multimodal reference data: Construct training samples that pair video clips with associated reference images, subject images, and audio clips to train the referenceconditioned generation capabilities. Construct editing pairs by applying transformations to source videos to produce (source, edit instruction, target) triplets for training the video editing capability. Construct extension pairs of consecutive clips for training video continuation.

 7.2 Training Stages

Implement a multistage training recipe:

1. Stage 1 — Largescale pretraining: Train the full model on texttovideo and imagetovideo tasks at lower resolution (480p) using the full dataset. Establish strong foundational generation quality, motion naturalness, physics compliance, and basic instruction following.

2. Stage 2 — Highresolution and joint audiovideo training: Continue training at 720p and introduce joint audiovideo generation. The audio and video latents must be cotrained jointly at this stage, not sequentially.

3. Stage 3 — Multimodal reference and editing training: Finetune on the referenceconditioned and editing datasets. Maintain a mixture of T2V/I2V samples to prevent degradation of foundational generation quality during this stage.

4. Stage 4 — Alignment and quality tuning: Apply a preference optimization or reward finetuning stage using humanpreference data. Optimize for: motion naturalness, audiovisual sync, aesthetic quality, instructionfollowing accuracy, and physical plausibility. Use a realism study methodology: collect evaluator judgments on whether generated outputs are distinguishable from real video footage and use these labels as reward signal.

 7.3 Loss Functions

Implement the following losses during training:

 Diffusion/flow matching denoising loss on both video and audio latent jointly.
 Consistency loss for editing tasks: penalize changes to nontargeted regions of the video during editing.
 Temporal consistency loss to enforce crossframe coherence of subject appearance and scene geometry.
 Audiovisual synchronization loss: enforce temporal alignment between audio events and corresponding visual events.
 Reference fidelity loss: enforce that subject appearance, motion rhythm, and style in the generated output match the provided reference inputs.



 8. Cinematographic and Directorial Reasoning

The model must not merely execute literal instructions — it must exhibit directorial reasoning capabilities:

 Shot planning: Given a long script or storyboard, the model must autonomously plan shot types (closeup, medium, wide, POV, crane, etc.), shot transitions, and editing rhythm without these being explicitly specified in the prompt.
 Camera movement: Support and accurately execute the following camera movements when instructed: dolly, zoom, pan, tilt, roll, rack focus, crane, handheld, steadicam. Support combined multiaxis movements.
 Cinematographic rules: The generated output must avoid 180degree rule violations, redundant coverage, mismatched shot sizes within a scene, and uneven pacing unless such violations are explicitly requested.
 Narrative coherence: For abstract or vague prompts, the model must generate a coherent narrative interpretation rather than producing a sequence of loosely related images.



 9. Evaluation Framework

Implement a comprehensive evaluation benchmark consisting of two tracks:

 9.1 Objective Evaluation

Implement automated evaluation pipelines for:

 Motion stability: Measure subject deformation rate, structural integrity across frames, jitter, and temporal smoothness using optical flowbased and pose estimationbased metrics.
 Prompt following accuracy: Measure semantic alignment between prompt and output for each of the following finegrained categories: holidays/festivals, consumer visual effects, counterreality instructions, cinematic visual effects, sametype interaction, crosstype interaction, group coordinated motion, advanced camera movement, special camera shots, editing rhythm, combined shot instructions, physical feedback, physical phenomena, natural phenomena, text overlay, short text generation, creative text generation, long script execution, abstract challenges, multientity feature matching, knowledge assessment, compound multiinstructions, surreal motion, intense sports motion, fine hand motion, anthropomorphic motion, emotion and expression, visual style, lighting and color tone, framing and composition.
 Aesthetic quality: Automated aesthetic scoring for: visual style, lighting, composition, object material texture, character detail fidelity, costume/prop design quality.
 Audio quality metrics: Measure audio expressiveness, multitrack layer richness, melody/tone alignment with prompt context.
 Audiovisual sync metrics: Measure lipsync accuracy, physical event sound offset (milliseconds), beatmatch score between music and visual editing rhythm.
 Generation consistency metrics for reference tasks: Measure subject identity preservation (face similarity, clothing detail match), motion rhythm alignment, style transfer fidelity, scene preservation during editing.

 9.2 Subjective Evaluation

Build a blind expert evaluation protocol:

 Recruit expert evaluators with professional background in advertising production and game/film production.
 Evaluate on a 1–5 rating scale for all dimensions listed in Section 9.1.
 Define usability rate as the fraction of outputs scoring ≥ 3, satisfaction rate as the fraction scoring ≥ 4, and delight rate as the fraction scoring 5.
 Run a realism study as a separate evaluation: present evaluators with interleaved real video clips and generated outputs and measure the model's ability to produce indistinguishable content.
 Evaluate narrative quality on three subdimensions: (1) cinematographic language — shot logic, expressiveness, absence of axiscrossing violations, matched shot sizing, even pacing; (2) plot design — coherence and engagement from vague prompts; (3) stylistic aesthetics — lighting, framing, composition, color grading, character/costume/prop/set consistency.

 9.3 Evaluation Dataset Construction

Construct specialized evaluation datasets for each task group:

 Reference evaluation set: samples covering subject reference, motion reference, visualeffect reference, and style reference.
 Editing evaluation set: samples covering subject editing, style editing, scene editing, and audio content editing.
 Extension evaluation set: forward and backward plot continuation samples.
 Combination evaluation set: paired tasks representing real production workflows.
 Sample distribution within each set must be tuned to minimize evaluation variance at small sample budgets.



 10. Inference and Fast Variant

 10.1 Standard Inference

Implement DDIMbased or flowmatching ODEbased inference with configurable number of denoising steps. Support batched multisample generation. The inference pipeline must accept the full structured input (text prompt, up to 3 video reference clips, up to 9 image references, up to 3 audio reference clips) and produce a final muxed audiovideo file.

 10.2 Accelerated Fast Variant

Implement a distilled or otherwise accelerated variant of the model for lowlatency scenarios. The fast variant must:

 Achieve substantially reduced inference time (target: 3–5× speedup over the standard model) through consistency distillation, step distillation, or another principled acceleration method.
 Maintain generation quality sufficient for productiongrade use cases — quality degradation must be bounded and quantified.
 Share the same interface and input/output specification as the standard model. No separate preprocessing or postprocessing pipelines.



 11. Safety Framework

Implement a structured safety assessment system integrated into the model lifecycle:

 Pregeneration filtering: Text and image prompt classifiers that detect and reject requests for: nonconsensual intimate content, identifiable real persons in harmful scenarios, content depicting minors in unsafe contexts, and content violating applicable legal standards.
 Postgeneration filtering: Video and audio classifiers applied to all model outputs before delivery. Flag and suppress outputs containing the above categories.
 Iterative redteam evaluation: Document a redteam evaluation protocol that is rerun at each training stage checkpoint and before each production deployment.
 Bias and fairness audit: Evaluate generated outputs for representation bias across gender, ethnicity, and age for all humansubject generation scenarios.

All safety components must be productiongrade, not placeholder classifiers.



 12. Deliverables

Deliver the following complete, unabridged, productionready components with no omissions:

1. Full model architecture implementation (tokenizers, encoders, main DiT backbone, decoder, audio module) with all weights initialization and training code.
2. Full data preprocessing pipeline (video ingestion, quality filtering, captioning, audio separation, multimodal pair construction, editing pair construction).
3. Full multistage training script with all loss functions, schedulers, and distributed training configuration.
4. Full inference pipeline supporting all task types (T2V, I2V, R2V, editing, extension, combination).
5. Full accelerated fastvariant distillation pipeline.
6. Full evaluation benchmark implementation (SeedVideoBench 2.0equivalent) with all objective metric pipelines and subjective evaluation tooling.
7. Full safety filtering pipeline (pre and postgeneration classifiers).
8. Comprehensive test suite covering all generation task types, all input modality combinations, edge cases (empty reference sets, maximum reference counts, minimum and maximum duration), and all evaluation categories listed in Section 9.1.

Every file must be complete. No file may contain the string "TODO", "placeholder", "mock", "dummy", "stub", "simulated", "fake", or equivalent. All configuration values must be concrete and justified in inline documentation.
